history.title: Count the Cubes

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Everybody learns to multiply length by width by height. Almost nobody gets told why that works. This week you find out, and after that the formula is something you could rebuild yourself.

1. Read **Filling Space**.
2. Learn the words in **Volume Words**, then win the **Crossword** and the **Matching** game.
3. Keep the **Three Ways to Find Volume** chart beside you.
4. Sort the cards in **Volume, Area, or Perimeter?**
5. Work through **Cube Problems** on paper.
6. Take **Volume Check**.
7. Lock it in with **Remember Why It Works**.
8. Read **Volume Questions Kids Ask**.
9. Finish with **Design: A Box That Wastes the Least**.

Your job this week: find a box at home and work out how many centimetre cubes would fill it. 📦

Picture panels: Build with unit cubes; Count complete layers; Add and compare solids; Inside space and outside covering. Artwork has no baked-in text. Use the native captions for dimensions and units. Gridded solids include hidden cubes; do not count visible faces as cubes. Gaps in the separated-layer diagram are only for display. Object illustrations are conceptual and must not be measured to calculate exact volumes. The tank water is below the rim, so the amount shown is less than full capacity. Sort area cards ask for surface coverage, and perimeter cards ask for boundary length. The packaging challenge uses ideal closed rectangular boxes: ignore material thickness, seams, tabs and waste, and treat rotations as the same dimensions. Educator review remains pending.

history.title: Filling Space
history.data:
## Filling Space

Here is a formula you have probably met: volume equals length times width times height. It works. But why should multiplying three numbers tell you anything about a box?

Start somewhere simpler. **Volume** is how much space a solid shape takes up. For solids built from cubes, we measure it by counting how many **unit** cubes fit inside, with no gaps and no overlaps. Other shapes may require parts of cubes or other methods. A unit cube is one centimetre on every edge, or one inch, or one metre. Whichever you pick, the answer comes out in **cubic** units, because you are counting cubes.

Now build a box out of cubes and watch what happens.

Lay one row along the bottom, four cubes long. Add rows beside it until the floor is covered. If the floor is 4 cubes by 3 cubes, that layer holds 12 cubes. The **area** of the base is 12 square units. A **layer** one unit high above that base contains 12 unit cubes and has volume 12 cubic units.

Now stack. Put an identical layer on top. Then another. If the box is 5 cubes tall, you have 5 layers of 12, which is 60.

That is the whole formula. Length times width gives you one layer. Multiplying by the height counts the layers. So l × w × h is not three random numbers multiplied. It is *cubes in a layer, times how many layers*.

Once you see it that way, a shortcut appears. Volume equals **base** area times height, for a prism or cylinder. Height means the perpendicular distance between the parallel bases.

What about an L-shaped solid made by joining rectangular **prisms**? Split it into non-overlapping rectangular prisms, find each volume, and add them. Not every solid can be split into rectangular prisms; a sloping roof, for example, may need a different method. Mathematicians call this **decomposing**, and it is the same move you already use with awkward shapes when finding area.

One last warning worth having. Volume is not the same as **capacity**, quite. Volume is the space a shape takes up. Capacity is how much a container holds. A thick-walled box has less capacity than its outside volume suggests, because the walls take up room too.

data.title: Remember Why It Works
data.instructions: Two cards hold the reasoning, not just the rule. Study the example, build one of your own, then say what it keeps straight.
data.sourceExcerpt: Length times width gives you one layer. Multiplying by the height counts the layers. So l x w x h is not three random numbers multiplied. It is cubes in a layer, times how many layers.

cards.target: Why multiplying three numbers gives you a volume
essentialFacts: Length times width gives the number of cubes in one layer.
For a layer one unit high, the cube count has the same numerical value as the base area in square units; the units differ.
Multiplying by the height counts how many layers there are.
So the formula is cubes in a layer, times layers.
cards.aiExample: Picture a rectangular stack of identical slices, each one unit thick. Find the volume of one slice, then multiply by the number of slices. If thickness changes, slice count alone no longer gives height in those units.
cards.mapping: The stack is an ideal model with matching layers and no gaps. A real loaf may have differently shaped ends or uneven slices. Layer thickness must be included when finding height.
cards.scaffoldStarter: One layer has volume ____. There are ____ matching layers, so total volume is ____.
scaffoldSteps: Think of something made of identical layers.
Say what counting the layers gives you.
coachPrompts: What would go wrong if the slices were different sizes?
cards.studentPrompt: Make your own layered picture for volume.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your picture show that the formula is really just counting?

hookFact.text: So l x w x h is not three random numbers multiplied. It is cubes in a layer, times how many layers.

cards.target: Why volume answers carry a small three
essentialFacts: Volume is measured by counting unit cubes.
A cube is measured in three directions, so the label is cubic.
Length is one direction, area is two, volume is three.
cards.aiExample: ONE, TWO, THREE: a line, a floor, a room. A line needs one measurement. A floor needs two. A room needs three. The small number is just how many directions you had to measure.
cards.mapping: Counting up one, two, three ties the exponent to something physical, so the small 3 stops being decoration and becomes a count of directions.

history.title: Cube Problems

problems.question: A box is 6 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm tall. What is its volume?

steps.explanation: Find one layer first. The base is 6 by 4, so one layer holds 6 x 4 = 24 cubes.
The box is 3 cubes tall, so there are 3 identical layers.
3 layers of 24 cubes is 72. The answer is 72 cubic cm, because you counted cubes.

problems.question: A prism has a base area of 15 square inches and a height of 4 inches. What is its volume?

steps.explanation: The base area is 15 square inches. A slice one inch thick has volume 15 cubic inches, even when the base cannot be tiled by whole one-inch cubes.
There are 4 layers, one for each inch of height.

problems.question: A box holds 120 cubic cm. Its base is 5 cm by 6 cm. How tall is it?

steps.explanation: The question is really: how many layers of 30 make 120?
120 divided by 30 is 4, so the box is 4 cm tall.

problems.question: An L-shaped solid is made of a 4 x 2 x 2 block joined to a 3 x 2 x 2 block. What is its volume?

steps.explanation: Decompose it. Handle each rectangular prism on its own.
First block: 4 x 2 x 2 = 16 cubic units.
Second block: 3 x 2 x 2 = 12 cubic units.
Add them: 16 + 12 = 28 cubic units. Nothing is counted twice because the blocks do not overlap.

problems.question: Two boxes both hold 36 cubic cm. One is 6 x 3 x 2 and the other is 9 x 2 x 2. Are they the same shape?
problems.answer: No, they are different shapes with the same volume

steps.explanation: Check the first: 6 x 3 x 2 = 36 cubic cm.
Check the second: 9 x 2 x 2 = 36 cubic cm. The volumes match.
But the edge lengths differ, so the boxes look nothing alike. Equal volume does not mean equal shape.

history.title: Volume Check

questions.question: Why does multiplying length by width by height give the volume?
options: Because three measurements always need multiplying together
Because volume is defined by that formula and cannot be shown
Because length times width is one layer, and height counts the layers
Because the three edges of a box are always equal to each other
questions.correctAnswer: Because length times width is one layer, and height counts the layers

questions.question: A prism has a base area of 20 square cm and is 3 cm tall. Its volume is:
options: 23 cubic cm
60 cubic cm
6.67 cubic cm
120 cubic cm

questions.question: Why are volume answers written in cubic units?
options: Because you are counting cubes that fit inside
Because cubes are the only solid shape in math
Because the answer is usually a very large number
Because it stops people confusing it with weight
questions.correctAnswer: Because you are counting cubes that fit inside
questions.conceptLabel: units come from what you count

questions.question: What is the best first move with an L-shaped solid?
options: Measure the longest edge and cube that number
Cut it into rectangular prisms and add their volumes
Find its perimeter and multiply that by the height
Round the shape to the nearest box and estimate
questions.correctAnswer: Cut it into rectangular prisms and add their volumes

questions.question: Two boxes have the same volume. What must also be true?
options: They must have the same edge lengths
They must have the same shape as each other
They must have the same base area exactly
Nothing else has to be true; only the space matches
questions.correctAnswer: Nothing else has to be true; only the space matches

questions.question: A box holds 90 cubic cm and its base is 5 cm by 6 cm. How tall is it? Show how you know.
questions.expectedAnswer: It is 3 cm tall. One layer is 5 x 6 = 30 cubes. The question is how many layers of 30 make 90, and 90 divided by 30 is 3.

questions.question: Explain the difference between the volume of a box and its capacity.
questions.expectedAnswer: Volume is the space the box itself takes up. Capacity is how much it can hold inside. A box with thick walls has less capacity than its outside volume suggests, because the walls take up room too.

history.title: Volume Questions Kids Ask

data.question: Does the formula work for a cylinder? 🥫
data.answer: Yes, in the layer form. Base area times height still holds, because a cylinder is the same circle all the way up. You just need the area of a circle first, which comes later.

data.question: What if the sides slant, like a pyramid? 🔺
data.answer: For a pyramid, base area times perpendicular height is too large because parallel cross-sections shrink toward the apex. A pyramid has one third the volume of a prism with the same base area and perpendicular height. It is not one third of just any surrounding box.

data.question: Can two different boxes hold the same amount?
data.answer: Easily. A 6 by 3 by 2 box and a 9 by 2 by 2 box both hold 36 cubic cm and look nothing alike. Same volume does not mean same shape.

data.question: Why do the units have that little 3? 🔢
data.answer: For a rectangular prism, multiplying three lengths multiplies their units too: cm × cm × cm = cubic cm, written cm³. A unit cube has one of those length units on each edge.

data.question: Is a litre a volume?
data.answer: Yes. One litre is exactly 1000 cubic centimetres. Litres and millilitres are just friendlier names for volumes you meet in a kitchen.

data.question: What if my measurements are in different units?
data.answer: Convert all lengths to the same unit before using the formula, so the result is easy to express in cubic units. Mixed units still have meaning, but need conversion: 1 cm × 1 m = 100 square cm.

history.title: Design: A Box That Wastes the Least
history.meta: 5th Grade • Design brief • fixed volume, least cardboard

data.title: A Box That Wastes the Least
data.instructions: Find every whole-number box that holds exactly the volume you are given. Then work out which one uses the least cardboard, and say why.
data.fitReason: Fixing the volume and varying the shape forces a student to separate volume from surface area, which is the confusion the standard is really guarding against, and it makes the answer arguable rather than looked up.

brief.context: A school club ships 48 unit cubes of soap. Compare ideal closed rectangular boxes with internal volume 48 cubic units. Use total surface area as the cardboard model, ignoring wall thickness, tabs, seams and cutting waste.
brief.audience: The club treasurer, who will approve the cheapest workable box
brief.drivingQuestion: Of all the whole-number boxes that hold exactly 48 unit cubes, which one uses the least cardboard, and is that the box the club should actually pick?
brief.seedDirection: List every whole-number set of three edges that multiplies to 48 before you calculate any surface area. There are fewer than you expect.
lockedLessonFacts: Volume is the number of unit cubes that fit inside with no gaps.
Length times width gives one layer, and height counts the layers.
Equal volume does not mean equal shape.
Every measurement must be in the same unit before you multiply.
openQuestions: How many different whole-number boxes hold exactly 48?
Does the box with the least cardboard have any other problem?
Would your answer change if the soaps were fragile?
stakeholders: The club treasurer paying for cardboard
Whoever has to pack the soaps by hand
The person carrying the finished box
criteria: A table of every whole-number box with volume 48, with its surface area
The volume of each box is shown to be 48, not just asserted
A recommendation with a reason, naming any tradeoff
At least four glossary words used correctly
constraints: Positive whole-number edge lengths only; rotations of the same three lengths count as one box
Exactly 48 cubic units inside; compare all six faces of each closed box, ignoring thickness, tabs, seams and waste
brief.deliverable: A table of every box that works with its surface area, a marked sketch of the one you recommend, and two sentences: why it wastes the least, and what you would give up by choosing it.
